claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins as a homogeneous high-temperature BCC phase.
Phase evolution during cooling in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is controlled by diffusion-mediated aluminum segregation.
Slow cooling allows aluminum atoms to segregate and locally order.
Aluminum segregation can produce a B2 or similar ordered secondary phase in this alloy.
Rapid quenching suppresses aluminum segregation by kinetically limiting diffusion.
Rapid quenching retains Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 as a single high-temperature BCC phase.
Cooling rate can substantially alter the number and identity of phases formed in a related high-entropy alloy.
In the cited Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy, slow cooling produces a more complex crystalline microstructure than accelerated cooling.
Slow-cooled Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 will contain secondary phases or ordered domains that are absent after rapid quenching.
The secondary phases or ordered domains in slow-cooled material will produce additional XRD peaks and TEM-visible microstructural features.
Aluminum segregation creates local compositional fluctuations that serve as nucleation sites for an ordered secondary phase.
The proposed mechanism operates only above a temperature at which aluminum mobility is significant.
At temperatures too low for significant aluminum diffusion, secondary-phase formation by the proposed mechanism should not occur.
Reducing the aluminum content can eliminate the driving force for segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Direct evidence for aluminum-driven ordering in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is currently lacking.
Absence of secondary-phase, local aluminum-enrichment, and ordering-calorimetry signatures in slow-cooled samples relative to quenched controls would falsify the proposed mechanism.
